title: The unknown god (Acts 17:22–31)
hook: in Athens Paul says in him we live and move and are

segments.voice: Yesterday, hymns, sung at midnight in the jail at Philippi by two beaten men. Your line was singing at midnight.

Athens. Even in Paul's day it was a kind of university town, famous for its past, full of temples, statues and people arguing in the marketplace. Paul is waiting there for his friends, walking the streets, and the city's statues stir him deeply. Philosophers hear him talking about Jesus and the resurrection and say, what is this babbler trying to say? So they bring him to the Areopagus, the hill where Athens heard new ideas, and ask him to explain. And Paul doesn't begin by attacking anyone.
screen: `ATHENS, A CITY OF ARGUMENTS.` → `WHAT IS THIS BABBLER SAYING?` → `UP TO THE AREOPAGUS.`

segments.voice: He begins with something he saw on his walk. Men of Athens, I see you are very religious. As I passed by, I found an altar with this inscription: "To the unknown God." What you worship without knowing, this I proclaim to you. That's his doorway: not their mistakes, but their own altar, their own honest admission that there was something they did not know. Then he describes God in words a Greek could follow. The God who made the world doesn't live in temples made by hands, and needs nothing from us, since he gives everyone life and breath. He made all nations from one, so that they would seek him, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him, though he is not far from any of us. Then the line, in the Douay-Rheims: "For in him we live, and move, and are." Paul even quotes their own poets: we are also his offspring. Those words come from the Greek poet Aratus, and Paul uses them to build a bridge. Only at the end does he speak of repentance, a day of judgment, and a man God raised from the dead. At the word resurrection, some laugh. Some say, we'll hear you again about this. And a few believe, including Dionysius, a member of the court, and a woman named Damaris. The Catholic Church draws on this speech when it teaches that other religions often reflect a ray of the truth, and that God is near to every person who seeks.
screen: `TO THE UNKNOWN GOD.` · `NOT FAR FROM ANY OF US.` · `IN HIM WE LIVE, AND MOVE, AND ARE.` · `SOME LAUGH, SOME BELIEVE.` · then, large: `WE ARE ALSO HIS OFFSPRING.`

segments.voice: Think about the culture around you this week, a song stuck in your head, a show, a piece of art, a sports moment, and look for an altar in it, so to speak: some longing, some question, some reach toward something bigger that it never quite names. Paul looked at a city full of statues and found a doorway; let one doorway in yours come to mind. If you pray, remember that in him we live, and move, and are, even here.
Areopagus. The hill in Athens where Paul was asked to explain his message, and where he began from an altar inscribed to an unknown god. Today's word.
Your line: in him we live. Tomorrow, needles and canvas in a workshop in Corinth. That's day five hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching, especially the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate, speaks with respect of what is true and holy in other religions, and Catholics remember Dionysius the Areopagite as a saint.

original.note: Greek: to an unknown god, the inscription Paul read on the altar.

trapdoor: what you thought: Paul argued the Greeks out of their beliefs.
what it means: he starts from their own altar and their own poets, telling them God is not far from any of us.
what a scholar hears: we are also his offspring is from Aratus's Phaenomena. and Dionysius the Areopagite later gave his name to writings composed centuries later by an unknown author.

chat.says: How did Paul start his speech in Athens? Did he attack their gods?
options: No, he began with their own altar to an unknown God: this I proclaim to you.
Yes, he told them their statues were worthless and must all be torn down.
He began with the resurrection, since that was what they most wanted to hear.
chat.meaning: Paul began from their altar to the unknown God and their own poets: God is not far from any of us. Only at the end did he speak of resurrection.

Areopagus.meaning: the hill where Athens heard new ideas

sources.quoted: For in him we live, and move, and are

notes: Confirm KJV 'TO THE UNKNOWN GOD' (printed in capitals in the KJV) and Douay-Rheims 17:28 'For in him we live, and move, and are'.
'In him we live and move' is sometimes attributed to Epimenides; the script names only Aratus for 'we are also his offspring'.
Nostra Aetate's 'ray of that Truth' is paraphrased, not quoted; confirm the framing doesn't rank traditions.
